stories.bridge: 2012 handed humanity the scissors; the frontier is deciding what to cut. Now let's learn CRISPR as a technology — and as the question it poses.
stories.hook: In June 2012, two scientists published a paper about a bacterial immune system — and handed humanity the scissors for DNA.
stories.narrative: Bacteria had been fighting viruses for billions of years, and their weapon was elegant: CRISPR arrays — genetic mugshots of past attackers — paired with the Cas9 protein, molecular scissors that cut any DNA matching the mugshot. Jennifer Doudna (UC Berkeley) and Emmanuelle Charpentier (then at Umeå University) weren't studying medicine; they were studying this bacterial trick. Their June 2012 Science paper showed the system could be reprogrammed: give Cas9 a synthetic guide RNA, and it would cut any DNA sequence you chose — in a test tube. The leap from test tube to living cells came fast: by early 2013, Feng Zhang's lab at the Broad Institute (and others) showed it worked in mammalian cells. The field exploded — thousands of labs, a patent war between Berkeley and Broad that ran for years, and in 2020 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Doudna and Charpentier, one of the fastest discoveries-to-Nobel in history. The applications followed the hype curve's real part: sickle-cell therapies approved, crops edited, diagnostics built. And the shadow: in 2018, He Jiankui's announcement of edited babies in China drew universal condemnation and a prison sentence — the frontier's reminder that capability outruns consensus. This module treats CRISPR as the template frontier technology: a natural mechanism, repurposed; a decade from paper to prize; power that demands governance. The scissors are real. The question — what may we cut — is the one you'll have to think about, not just the technique. The patent war — Berkeley versus the Broad Institute — ran for years and reshaped how universities value biotech IP, while the science marched on regardless. The first approved therapies (for sickle cell, 2023) proved the medicine real. In this module, CRISPR is the template for reading any frontier: the mechanism, the timeline from paper to product, and the governance question that arrives with the capability. The scissors don't decide; we do.

stories.bridge: Feynman's challenge still stands: build the machine that nature requires. Now let's learn what a qubit actually is — and why it's so hard to keep one alive.
stories.hook: In 1981, Richard Feynman told a conference: nature isn't classical — so our computers shouldn't be either.
stories.narrative: The occasion was the first Conference on the Physics of Computation at MIT's Endicott House. Feynman, thinking about simulating quantum systems — molecules, materials, the stuff of chemistry — pointed out the fundamental mismatch: a classical computer needs exponentially growing resources to simulate a quantum system, because the system's state space doubles with every particle. His proposal, published as 'Simulating Physics with Computers' in 1982: build a computer that is itself quantum, so the simulation is natural. In 1985, David Deutsch at Oxford formalized the idea, defining the quantum Turing machine and the notion of quantum computation as a discipline. Then in 1994, Peter Shor — at Bell Labs — dropped the bombshell: a quantum algorithm that factors large numbers exponentially faster than any known classical method. Since RSA encryption depends on factoring being hard, Shor's algorithm meant a large quantum computer would break the internet's locks — and the race was on, funded by that threat as much as by the promise. The decades since have been engineering trench warfare against decoherence: superconducting qubits, trapped ions, error correction — the qubit wants to be quantum, the universe wants it classical. Feynman's 1981 intuition remains the field's compass: don't fight nature's mathematics, compute with it. This module teaches the basics — superposition, entanglement, the qubit — as the physics Feynman said we'd need. The machine is still being born; you're learning its first language. The engineering war since has been against decoherence — superconducting loops, trapped ions, topological bets — with error correction as the long game: thousands of physical qubits per logical one. Feynman's 1981 point stands untouched: the universe computes quantumly, and matching its mathematics is the only way to simulate it. In this module you'll learn the qubit as physics first, hype last — the frontier method applied to the hardest hardware problem alive.
stories.title: The story behind the quantum computer
verifiedClaims: Feynman's 'Simulating Physics with Computers' came from the 1981 MIT conference

stories.bridge: Ignition was the physics milestone; the engineering milestone — net electricity, affordably — is still ahead. Now let's learn the real status: what's been proven, and what hasn't.
stories.hook: In the early hours of December 5, 2022, 192 lasers fired in Livermore, California — and fusion finally paid for itself.
stories.narrative: The National Ignition Facility is the largest laser system ever built: 192 beams converging on a peppercorn-sized pellet of deuterium and tritium. For over a decade, NIF had chased ignition — the point where the fusion reaction produces more energy than the lasers delivered to the target. Shot after shot fell short, and critics called the facility a boondoggle. Then, on December 5, 2022, a shot with refined target design and a touch more laser energy crossed the line: about 3.15 megajoules of fusion energy from about 2.05 megajoules delivered — scientific breakeven, Q greater than one, the first controlled fusion reaction to pay for itself in the lab. The Department of Energy announced it on December 13, 2022, to global headlines. The honest accounting matters for this module: the gain was measured against laser energy on target, not the hundreds of megajoules the facility consumed to fire the lasers — wall-plug breakeven is far off, and NIF fires a few shots a day while a power plant would need ten per second. Fusion has been 'thirty years away' for seventy years, and ignition didn't change the engineering mountain — it proved the mountain is climbable. Private fusion companies have since raised billions on that proof. This module's job is the frontier method applied: separate the milestone from the hype, track what's actually been demonstrated, and watch the right metrics. December 5, 2022, is real. Everything after is the race. The private race is the new chapter: Commonwealth Fusion, Helion, and dozens of startups have raised billions on approaches NIF never tried — compact tokamaks, field-reversed configurations — betting that the physics proof unlocks engineering sprints. Whether any of them reaches the grid is the open question this module tracks. Ignition proved the mountain climbable; the startups are arguing about the route.
stories.title: The story behind fusion ignition
verifiedClaims: NIF achieved scientific breakeven on December 5, 2022 (3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ)

stories.bridge: Moore's metronome is slowing; the frontier is what replaces it. Now let's learn semiconductor scaling — the physics, the economics, and the beyond-Moore bets.

figures.name: Gordon Moore
figures.role: Co-founder of Intel; formulated Moore's law (1965)

stories.hook: In April 1965, Gordon Moore noticed the number of transistors on a chip was doubling every year — and wrote it down.
stories.narrative: Moore was Fairchild Semiconductor's R&D director when Electronics magazine asked him to predict the next decade of integrated circuits. Looking at the data — from a handful of transistors in 1959 to 64 in 1965 — he observed the doubling pattern and projected it forward ten years, to 65,000 transistors by 1975. It was an observation, not a law of physics — but the industry treated it as a roadmap, then a self-fulfilling prophecy: chipmakers planned to the cadence, equipment makers built to it, and the doubling held for decades. In 1975 Moore revised it to every two years, the version most people quote. The economic half was as important as the technical: each generation halved the cost per transistor, which is why computing got exponentially cheaper as it got exponentially more powerful — the engine of the digital age. Moore co-founded Intel in 1968 and watched his observation become the industry's metronome for fifty years. The metronome is now slowing: transistors are atomic-scale, fabs cost twenty billion dollars, and the easy doublings are over — which is exactly why this module exists. The frontier bets — chiplets, 3D stacking, new materials, new architectures, and the quantum machines from the last story — are all answers to the question Moore's law leaves behind: what drives progress when the doubling stops? Moore gave the industry its rhythm; your generation writes the next bar. The law's real content was economic as much as technical: each generation halved the cost per transistor, funding the next generation's fab. That flywheel — now straining at $20 billion per fab — is why the frontier bets matter: chiplets, 3D stacking, photonics, new architectures. In this module you'll learn to read the post-Moore landscape the way Moore read 1965: as data, not destiny. Read the landscape as data, not destiny.
